items.answer: pH

items.stem: Explain why pure water is neutral at all temperatures even though its pH changes.
items.answer: In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] always, so it is neutral; Kw increases with temperature (dissociation is endothermic), so [H⁺] increases and pH decreases below 7.
items.markingKey: [H⁺] = [OH⁻] [1]; Kw increases with T, so pH falls [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why 0.10 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid has a higher pH than 0.10 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: Ethanoic acid is weak and only partially dissociates, so [H⁺] is much lower than 0.10 mol dm⁻³; HCl dissociates fully.
items.markingKey: partial vs full dissociation [1]; lower [H⁺] [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf compares solutions of 0.05 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid and 0.05 mol dm⁻³ chloroethanoic acid (Ka = 1.38 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³) at 298 K. (c) Suggest a simple test, other than pH, to distinguish between the two solutions.
items.answer: (a) 16.61% (b) Both contain the same number of moles of acid (monoprotic, same concentration); as OH⁻ removes H⁺, the weak acid equilibrium shifts to release more H⁺ until all the acid reacts. (c) Add magnesium ribbon (or calcium carbonate): the strong acid gives faster effervescence; or measure electrical conductivity (higher for HCl).

items.stem: Explain why diluting a strong acid by a factor of 10 increases the pH by 1, but diluting a weak acid by 10 increases the pH by only about 0.5.
items.answer: For a strong acid [H⁺] falls by 10 times. For a weak acid [H⁺] = √(Ka × c), so [H⁺] falls by √10 (and dilution increases the fraction dissociated).
items.markingKey: strong: [H⁺] ÷ 10 [1]; weak: √(Ka c) relation [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a mixture of ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate acts as a buffer.
items.answer: Large reservoirs of CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻; added H⁺ combines with CH₃COO⁻ to form CH₃COOH; added OH⁻ reacts with CH₃COOH to form CH₃COO⁻ and water; the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes very little so pH stays nearly constant.
items.markingKey: large amounts of HA and A⁻ [1]; H⁺ removed by A⁻ [1]; OH⁻ removed by HA [1]; ratio nearly constant [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain how the carbonic acid–hydrogencarbonate buffer controls the pH of blood.
items.answer: H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; extra H⁺ (e.g. lactic acid) combines with HCO₃⁻ to form H₂CO₃, which forms CO₂ removed in the lungs; extra OH⁻ reacts with H₂CO₃; pH stays at about 7.4.
items.markingKey: equilibrium [1]; response to H⁺ [1]; response to OH⁻ [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain the common ion effect using silver chloride and sodium chloride as an example.
items.answer: AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq); adding NaCl increases [Cl⁻]; to keep [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = Ksp the equilibrium shifts left, AgCl precipitates and its solubility decreases.

items.stem: Explain why Ksp values are only used for sparingly soluble salts.

items.stem: Explain why several small extractions are more efficient than one large one.
items.answer: Each extraction removes a fraction of the remaining solute; repeating with fresh solvent removes a fraction of what is left each time, so the total removed is greater for the same total volume.

items.stem: Ethan wants to extract an organic product from an aqueous reaction mixture using a separating funnel and an immiscible organic solvent. (a) Explain why the organic solvent must be immiscible with water. (b) Explain how the polarity of a solute affects its partition coefficient between octan-1-ol and water. (c) Suggest why the extraction is repeated several times with small volumes of solvent.
items.answer: (a) So that two layers form and can be separated; the product distributes between them according to Kpc. (b) Non-polar solutes are more soluble in octan-1-ol (larger Kpc); polar or ionic solutes that hydrogen-bond with water are more soluble in water (smaller Kpc). (c) More solute is extracted in total for the same total volume of solvent.

Omar compares solutions of 0.1 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid and 0.1 mol dm⁻³ propanoic acid (Ka = 1.35 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³) at 298 K. (a) Calculate the pH of each solution. (b) Calculate the percentage of propanoic acid molecules that are dissociated. (c) Explain why the two acids need the same volume of NaOH for neutralisation even though their pH values differ. (d) Calculate pKa for the weak acid.
items.answer: (a) HCl: 1; propanoic acid: 2.93 (b) 1.16% (c) Both contain the same number of moles of acid (monoprotic, same concentration); as OH⁻ removes H⁺, the weak acid equilibrium shifts to release more H⁺ until all the acid reacts. (d) 4.87

items.answer: (a) Initial pH about 2.9; vertical section about pH 7.5–10.5 at 25.0 cm³; final pH about 13. (b) A pH meter gives the pH at every point, so the half-equivalence pH (= pKa) can be read from the curve; an indicator only shows the end point.
